sections.body_md:
An extended measurement update is the linear update with the measurement rebuilt at the current estimate. The sensor is a nonlinear map. The first-order model of that map is the map's value plus its Jacobian times the displacement from the estimate. The innovation is the reading minus the map's value, not minus the Jacobian times the estimate. The gain is the linear gain with the Jacobian standing where the measurement row would stand. The variance update uses that same Jacobian.

The Jacobian has to be new whenever the estimate moves. A square-law sensor has derivative twice the position, so a correction that changes the position changes the derivative. Using yesterday's Jacobian on today's estimate is a frozen linear model.

The step is exact for the tangent model and the quadratic prior, and only approximate for the curved sensor. If the tangent is a poor picture of the map, the correction can land far from a point that zeros the nonlinear stationarity condition. A position estimate with a square-law reading is the concrete case: each new reading is linearized at the latest position, and the next reading starts over.

sections.heading: Key equations
sections.body_md:
With Jacobian \(J_h\) at the estimate,
\[
L = \frac{P J_h}{J_h^2 P + R},
\]
the innovation is the reading minus \(h\) at the estimate, and the variance update is \((1 - L J_h) P\).

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.body_md:
Take a position estimate of \(5\) with variance \(1\), and a sensor that reports the square of position. The map equals \(25\) and the Jacobian equals \(10\). A reading of \(45\) with measurement variance \(20\) has innovation \(20\). The innovation variance is \(100 + 20 = 120\), so the gain is \(10/120\). The correction is that gain times \(20\).

The dock position is 6.66667. The Jacobian at this new position is no longer \(10\). The next reading has to be linearized again. The nonlinear cost, prior plus squared sensor residual, does not have zero derivative at this position, because the step minimized the tangent model rather than the curved sensor.

sections.heading: Common pitfalls
sections.body_md: Putting the Jacobian in the innovation, in place of the map, is the linear residual of a map that passes through the origin. A square law does not. A second slip is to use the estimate itself as the Jacobian of \(u^2\). The derivative is twice the estimate. A third is to update the variance with \(1 - L\) when the Jacobian is not \(1\). The factor that multiplies the gain is the Jacobian. A fourth is to keep a single linearization for every later block. The derivative of a nonlinear sensor moves with the estimate.

sections.heading: Where this leads
sections.body_md: The same tangent step, pointed at a root of a map rather than at a measurement update, is Newton's method. The next guess is where the tangent hits zero, and a tangent drawn at a poor point can send that guess far away. An extended update has the prior variance to soften the step. A pure root iteration does not, which is why the starting point matters even more there.
